items.title: Tessaline Forms 5.0: signal-based forms, async validators and a new migration path
items.text: Tessaline Forms 5.0 is now available on npm. This major release of our form library for Angular rebuilds the form model on top of Angular signals: every control now exposes value, status and errors as read-only signals, and the previous observable streams are kept behind a compatibility flag until version 6.0. Async validators can now be cancelled automatically when the value changes again; in our benchmark of a 200-field form, this reduced redundant HTTP validation calls by 63%. The release also adds typed form arrays, a debounce option per control, and server-side rendering support for error messages. Breaking changes: the FormStateService class is removed (deprecated since 4.2), the minimum supported Angular version is now 21.0, and the default update strategy changes from 'change' to 'blur' for text inputs. An automated migration is provided through ng update and covers the FormStateService removal but not the update strategy change, which must be reviewed manually. Version 4.x will receive security fixes until June 2027. Known limitation: file inputs are not yet supported by the signal model and still use the legacy API.

items.title: Introducing Nembra-V2, our open-weights vision-language model
items.text: Today we are releasing Nembra-V2, the second version of our vision-language model, with open weights under the Apache-2.0 license. Nembra-V2 has 12 billion parameters and accepts images, PDF pages and text as input; it produces text only. Compared with Nembra-V1, the context window grows from 32,000 to 128,000 tokens. On the DocVQA benchmark, Nembra-V2 scores 91.2, up from 84.5 for Nembra-V1. On ChartQA it scores 79.8. The model runs on a single 24 GB GPU with 4-bit quantization, at about 35 tokens per second in our tests. The weights, the inference code and a model card are published today; the training code is not released. The training data mixes licensed datasets and data generated by our previous models; the model card lists the sources. Limitations: Nembra-V2 does not process video or audio, its accuracy drops on handwritten documents, and it was evaluated in English and French only. A hosted API will open in December at a price that has not been announced.

items.title: Korvo 2.4: durable checkpoints for long-running agents
items.text: Korvo 2.4 adds durable checkpoints: the state of each agent step is persisted to SQLite or Postgres, and an interrupted agent resumes from its last completed step instead of restarting. Tool calls already executed are not replayed. The release also fixes two memory leaks in the streaming client and drops support for Node 18.

items.title: Security advisory: workspace escape in Halvard agent runtime tool sandbox
items.text: A flaw in the Halvard agent runtime file tool lets a prompt-injected agent read files outside its workspace through symbolic links. Versions 1.6.0 to 1.8.2 are affected. Version 1.8.3 fixes the issue. Users who cannot upgrade should disable the file tool.

items.title: Why I stopped letting coding agents write my tests
items.text: For six months I let coding agents write most of the tests in my team's Angular codebase. Coverage went up from 61% to 84%, but the number of production bugs did not go down. Looking back at a sample of 120 generated tests, I found that 40 of them only asserted what the implementation already did, including two tests that locked in known bugs. My conclusion is not that agents are useless for testing. I now write the test cases myself, as plain-language scenarios, and let the agent turn them into code. I also ask the agent to write a failing test first when it fixes a bug. This is one team's experience, not a study, and I would like to see better data on how generated tests affect defect rates.
